title: Specify password for SSL client side certificate

messages.content: I'm looking into GitHub issue #1573 regarding the inability to provide a password for SSL client certificates in requests. Currently, passing a tuple to 'cert' only supports (cert_path, key_path), but it doesn't account for encrypted private keys. How should we handle this in the Session.request() flow?

This is a valid point. The underlying 'urllib3' library manages SSL contexts, but we need to expose an interface in 'requests/sessions.py' to handle this. We might need to extend the 'cert' parameter to accept a tuple of three: (cert_path, key_path, password). I'll start by investigating 'requests/adapters.py' where the 'cert_verify' logic resides.

I've checked 'requests/adapters.py'. The 'HTTPAdapter.cert_verify' method currently unpacks the cert into just two parts. If I change the unpacking logic to support a 3-tuple, I'll need to pass that password down to the 'urllib3' pool manager. Is 'urllib3' prepared to handle a 'key_password' argument in its connection pool options?

Good catch. Looking at the 'urllib3' documentation, the 'ssl_wrap_socket' utility does accept a 'key_file' and 'key_password'. I suggest we modify 'requests/adapters.py' within the 'cert_verify' method to identify if the third element exists and pass it into the 'poolmanager' initialization. Let's start by adding a test case in 'tests/test_requests.py' to trigger a password-protected key error.

I've added the test case, and it fails as expected with a 'TypeError' during 'ssl.SSLContext.load_cert_chain' because the private key is encrypted. I'm currently modifying 'requests/adapters.py' to update the 'cert_verify' function to extract the password and store it in the adapter's configuration.

That seems like the correct path. Once you have the password extracted in the adapter, you need to ensure it persists correctly when 'HTTPAdapter.send()' is called. Check the 'self.poolmanager' configuration to ensure the 'key_password' is being correctly passed through during the 'urllib3' connection object creation.

Wait, I noticed that 'HTTPAdapter' caches connection pools. If I update the configuration in 'send()', will the existing connection pool be invalidated? I might need to force a pool refresh if the certificate parameters change.

That is an excellent observation. The 'poolmanager' is indeed persistent. You should implement a logic in 'HTTPAdapter.get_connection' that checks if the 'cert' tuple has changed from the one used to create the pool. If it has, we might need to clear the pool or recreate it to avoid SSL handshake failures.

Implementing a check in 'get_connection' sounds invasive. Is there a cleaner way? Maybe we can include the password in the connection key dictionary used by 'urllib3' so that different certificates or passwords trigger distinct pools?

Using the connection key approach in 'HTTPAdapter' is definitely more 'requests'-idiomatic. By including the 'cert' parameter in the pool key, 'urllib3' will naturally handle pool separation for us. Go ahead and adjust 'requests/adapters.py' to include the password in the key generation logic.

I've updated the 'cert_verify' logic to properly handle the 3-tuple and adjusted the 'pool_connections' logic. Testing against a local server with a password-protected .pem, I'm now getting a successful handshake! However, the 'requests' documentation in 'docs/user/advanced.rst' needs to be updated to reflect this new feature.

Great work on the functional fix! Make sure the documentation explicitly mentions that the third element of the 'cert' tuple is optional. Also, consider adding a backward-compatibility check so that existing 2-tuple configurations don't break.

I added the backward-compatibility check by using 'if len(cert) == 3' and setting 'password' to 'None' by default. The existing tests in 'tests/test_requests.py' passed, confirming that legacy usage remains unaffected. I'll now draft the documentation update.

Looks solid. Before we finalize, can you run the full suite using 'pytest' to ensure no side effects on HTTPS connection pooling? Especially check for any 'SSLError' exceptions during concurrent requests.

Running the full suite now. I encountered one failure in 'test_https_proxy_with_cert'. It seems the proxy handling code also expects a 2-tuple for certs. I'll need to patch 'requests/adapters.py' to propagate the password support to proxy-based connections as well.

Ah, proxies. Yes, the 'proxy_manager' also uses the certificate parameters for authentication. You'll need to pass the password through the 'proxy_args' dictionary in the 'HTTPAdapter' initialization. Keep it consistent with how the main connection handles it.

That did it. I updated 'HTTPAdapter' to pass the password to both the standard connection pool and the proxy manager. 'pytest' is now showing a 100% pass rate. The password is correctly passed to 'urllib3', and connections are isolated correctly.

That is excellent news. You've effectively covered the client-side certificate password support. Could you push the code to a branch and open a PR? I'd like to perform a final review of the diff in 'requests/adapters.py' to ensure no sensitive memory leaks of the password string.

Good call on memory safety. I've ensured the password isn't logged in any debug output within 'adapters.py'. Everything looks ready for merge. Thanks for the guidance on the 'poolmanager' keying strategy!

You're very welcome. The 'poolmanager' approach was definitely the right architectural decision to keep connection pooling efficient. I'll review your PR #1573 shortly. Great job closing out this long-standing issue for the community.

I've just pushed the PR #1573. I double-checked the logic in 'requests/adapters.py' to ensure that the password isn't exposed in the connection pool key, preventing any accidental leaks. Are there any specific integration tests I should add to ensure this continues to work as the library evolves?

Good catch on the connection pool key. You definitely don't want the password in the key string. For integration tests, I'd suggest creating a specific test case in 'tests/test_requests.py' that generates a temporary password-protected PEM file using 'cryptography' or 'pyOpenSSL' within the test lifecycle, and verify that a request succeeds.

That sounds like a robust approach. I'll use the 'pytest' 'tmpdir' fixture to handle the temporary PEM creation. Should I mock the 'ssl' context or perform an actual local server handshake to ensure the password decryption path is fully exercised?

An actual loopback handshake is always superior to mocking for security features like this. Since we rely on 'urllib3', testing against a local 'http.server' with a custom 'ssl.SSLContext' will prove that the certificate loading actually triggers the password decryption correctly.

I've implemented the loopback test. However, the 'test_session_with_cert_password' is intermittently failing with a 'PermissionError' when trying to cleanup the temporary certificate file on Windows. Any tips on handling file locking in the test environment?

Ah, the classic Windows file handle leak. This usually happens if the SSL context doesn't close the file descriptor immediately. Try manually closing the file handle after loading the context or wrapping the creation in a 'contextlib.closing' block to ensure the handle is released before you attempt the teardown.

Wrapping the file handle in 'contextlib.closing' solved the Windows cleanup issue. I'm now getting consistent passes across all OS platforms in the CI runner. Should I squash these commits before merging or keep the history of the fix?

Let's keep the history clean by squashing the fixes related to the 'HTTPAdapter' and the new test suite into one logical commit. It makes the git log much easier to audit for future security regressions.

Squashing complete. The commit message now clearly references #1573 and highlights the transition to supporting a 3-tuple in the 'cert' parameter. Should I also run the linter 'flake8' to ensure my changes comply with the project standards?

Definitely run 'flake8'. Also, run 'black --check' if the repo uses it. You want to make sure the indentation on the tuple unpacking inside 'adapters.py' doesn't violate any style guides. Consistency is key for the core maintainers.

Ran 'flake8' and 'black', everything came back clean. The variable names in 'get_adapter' match the existing style. I'm feeling confident about the state of this feature. Are there any final edge cases with different 'urllib3' versions I should worry about?

Good question. Make sure your 'setup.py' or 'requirements.txt' reflects the minimum version of 'urllib3' that supports the 'password' argument in its 'SSLContext' wrappers. If someone uses an ancient version, they might get a 'TypeError'.

I checked the dependencies. It looks like we need 'urllib3 >= 1.9' to support this properly. I will update the documentation to note this version requirement clearly so users don't encounter unexpected errors when they update.
Perfect. Adding that note to 'docs/user/advanced.rst' will save the support team a lot of headache. Once you update that, I think the code is ready for the maintainers to pull.

Done. I've updated the docs and added a note about the 'urllib3' version dependency. I’m re-running the test suite one last time to confirm everything is still green. Any final advice before I mark the PR as ready for review?

Just perform one final manual check: if a user provides an incorrect password, does it raise a clear 'SSLError' or 'OpenSSL.crypto.Error'? You want to ensure the error message is descriptive, not just a generic connection failure.

Tested that. It raises 'OpenSSL.SSL.Error', which is caught and wrapped as an 'SSLError'. The error message explicitly mentions 'bad decrypt', which is helpful for users troubleshooting their PEM files. That seems sufficient.
That is exactly what a user would need to debug their config. You've handled the implementation, the edge cases, the documentation, and the error reporting. The PR looks very professional.
Thanks! I've marked the PR as ready for review and notified the maintainers. It feels great to see this feature move from issue to solution. I appreciate all the help on the 'HTTPAdapter' logic.
It was my pleasure. You tackled a complex piece of the 'requests' internals with a clean, backward-compatible solution. This will definitely be a welcomed addition by the community.

One of the maintainers commented on the PR. They noticed that while 'cert=(cert_path, key_path)' works, they want to see if we can support a tuple for the key path that includes the password, like 'cert=(cert_path, (key_path, password))'. Is that a cleaner API for us?

That is a common pattern in other libraries. It avoids adding a new argument to the 'request' method. You would need to update the logic in 'requests/sessions.py' inside the 'request' method to check if the second element of the 'cert' tuple is another tuple, signaling the password is included.

That makes sense. If I modify 'requests/adapters.py' to unpack that tuple, I can pass the password to 'self.cert_file'. I will update the 'HTTPAdapter.cert_verify' method to handle this structured input. It definitely feels more idiomatic for 'requests'.

Great idea. Don't forget to update the docstrings in 'requests/api.py' to reflect that 'cert' now accepts a tuple for the key file. It keeps the API surface area small while being highly discoverable for users.

I've drafted the change. In 'requests/adapters.py', I'm now checking 'if isinstance(cert, tuple) and len(cert) == 2 and isinstance(cert[1], tuple)'. It feels robust enough to handle existing users while providing the new functionality. Running tests now.
The check looks safe. Ensure you run the existing test suite for 'test_requests.py' to make sure you didn't break standard file-path based certificates. Backward compatibility is king here.

Tests passed, but I hit a slight snag. When the user passes just a string for the cert, the logic needs to explicitly fall back to the old behavior. I've updated the 'cert_verify' method to handle the string, the flat tuple, and the nested tuple.

Good catch. Sometimes simple 'if/else' blocks are easier to maintain than complex type-checking logic. Are you writing a specific test case in 'tests/test_adapters.py' for this nested tuple structure?

Yes, I just added 'test_cert_with_password_tuple'. It mocks the 'urllib3' call and verifies that the password is correctly extracted and passed down. It's working perfectly. I'll push this updated commit now.
The PR activity is picking up. A maintainer just gave a '+1'. They were particularly impressed with how you handled the nested tuple parsing without creating a breaking change.
That's great news! I feel much better about this API than the previous approach of potentially adding an 'auth' parameter, which might have conflicted with other authentication schemes.
It really is the cleanest solution. Do you think we need to update the examples in the 'README.rst' file to showcase this new tuple syntax, or is it better to leave it in 'advanced.rst'?
I'll put a brief mention in 'README.rst' for discoverability, but keep the detailed explanation in 'docs/user/advanced.rst'. That seems like the right balance for user visibility.
Excellent strategy. Keeping the README light is a good practice for library maintenance. Did you check if the 'requests' version should be bumped in 'setup.py' given this is a new feature?

Since this is a minor feature, I'll recommend bumping the minor version. I updated the 'VERSION' file locally to reflect that. The CI build is green, and the maintainer is waiting on the documentation update.
You've really gone the extra mile here. From addressing the GitHub issue #1573 to refactoring the API to be more idiomatic, this has been a textbook example of open-source contribution.
Thanks for your guidance through the process. It was daunting looking at the 'HTTPAdapter' source code at first, but it makes much more sense now that I've mapped out the call stack.
You're very welcome. That 'HTTPAdapter' is the backbone of the library, so knowing it well is definitely a badge of honor. Ready to merge?
Ready. I just pushed the final documentation changes. Marking as ready for final merge. Hopefully, this helps everyone who had trouble with their encrypted PEM files.
It will definitely help. You've closed the gap on a long-standing request. Well done, and I look forward to your next contribution to the project.

I noticed in the latest CI logs for my pull request that a flaky test in test_requests.py is failing intermittently. It seems related to the SSL handshake timeout when using the password-protected cert. Could this be a race condition during the test setup?

That is frustrating. Flaky tests in test_requests.py are usually timing issues with the local SSL server fixture. Let's look at the fixture implementation in tests/test_requests.py. Is it possible the server isn't waiting long enough for the client to parse the encrypted key?

Good catch. I found the helper function in tests/utils.py that spins up the server. It uses a sleep(0.1) before starting the SSL handshake. I'll bump that to 0.5 to see if it stabilizes the environment.

Increasing the sleep is a reasonable diagnostic step. If that fixes it, we should ideally replace the sleep with a proper retry loop using a timeout mechanism in the test setup to avoid polluting the test suite with magic numbers.

I refactored the test to use a simple 'while' loop with a timeout in conftest.py. Running the suite again, all 400+ tests passed, including the new SSL password test case. That feels much more robust than the sleep hack.
Excellent work. Robust testing is just as important as the feature itself. Does the coverage report in the GitHub Actions dashboard show any gaps in the new code paths within adapters.py?
Checking the coverage report now. It looks like the 'cert_file' error handling branch in adapters.py is at 100%. I'm feeling confident about the merge now. Should I squash my commits?
Yes, squashing into a clean commit with a descriptive message referencing 'Closes #1573' is standard practice here. It keeps the history of the requests repository clean and readable.
Done. Squashed the commits and pushed to the branch. I also updated the changelog.md file as requested by the maintainers. Anything else before I trigger the final review?
You are all set. You've addressed the issue, verified the implementation, refactored for stability, and handled documentation and changelogs. That is a complete contribution cycle.
I'm looking at the GitHub pull request interface. Should I include a summary of the test changes in the PR description, or just keep it focused on the SSL feature?
Definitely include it. Mentions of the stability improvements in tests/test_requests.py demonstrate that you care about the project's health, not just your specific patch.
Good advice. Added a section titled 'Test Stability Improvements' to the PR. I'm hitting the 'Request Review' button now. It feels strange to see it finally marked as 'Ready for Review'.
That's the best feeling in open source. Just keep an eye on your notifications for any final comments from the maintainers. Don't be surprised if they request a minor stylistic change.
I'll keep a close watch. If a maintainer requests a change in the code style for the SSL password decryption logic, I'm ready to pivot quickly.
Your preparation shows. By the way, have you considered how this might affect users on older versions of OpenSSL? I recall some older versions having issues with specific encrypted PEM formats.
I actually added a check for the OpenSSL version in the requests/adapters.py module initialization. If the version is too old, it throws a clear 'NotImplementedError' instead of a cryptic crash.
That is highly defensive and exactly the kind of polish we look for. You've really elevated the quality of this implementation beyond the original issue requirements.
Thanks again for all your help. It's been a long journey from that initial comment to this finalized code, but I've learned a ton about how the request pipeline works.
It has been a pleasure to mentor you through this. You've demonstrated great engineering instincts. Let me know when you decide on your next contribution, and I'll be here to review.

I just received a notification on the PR. The maintainer pointed out that my check in requests/adapters.py might be too restrictive. They want me to handle the legacy OpenSSL case by gracefully failing the certificate load rather than raising an error globally. How should I approach modifying the session initialization?

That is a fair critique. Instead of failing on import in requests/adapters.py, you should handle this inside the HTTPAdapter.cert_verify method. Try wrapping the key loading block in a try-except and logging a warning instead of halting execution.

Makes sense. I'll move the logic inside the cert_verify call. I'm looking at requests/adapters.py now. I'll replace the global NotImplementedError with a conditional logging statement that warns the user if the password field is provided but the OpenSSL version is too ancient.

Sounds solid. Remember to import the logging module at the top of requests/adapters.py. Also, ensure you aren't silencing the actual exception; just log it and fallback to standard unencrypted behavior if possible.

I've drafted the change. I'm now using logging.warning in requests/adapters.py. I'm running the test suite in tests/test_requests.py to ensure the password handling still works on modern systems despite the new safety checks.
Perfect. Check the output of py.test -v tests/test_requests.py. Specifically, verify that tests involving invalid or legacy PEM files don't hang or exit with a non-zero code unexpectedly.
The tests passed. I've pushed the update to the branch. The maintainer also asked me to document this behavior in the docs/user/advanced.rst file. Is there a standard way to write these notes?

Look at how other SSL options are documented in docs/user/advanced.rst. Follow their reStructuredText format. Add a small 'SSL Client Password' subsection mentioning that password protection requires a modern OpenSSL.

I've updated docs/user/advanced.rst and it looks consistent with the rest of the documentation. I'm feeling confident about these docs changes. Should I squash my commits before the maintainer reviews again?
Usually, yes. Keep your commit history clean. Use git rebase -i to combine the fix-up commits into one coherent 'Add support for password-protected client certificates' commit.
Done. I squashed everything into one clean commit. The CI pipeline on GitHub is re-running the tests in tests/test_requests.py and tests/test_auth.py. I'll wait for that to turn green.
The CI pipeline is the final barrier. Once it passes, you've essentially done all you can. Is there anything else in the issue tracker regarding SSL that you might want to look into?
Actually, I noticed some people complaining about certificate chain verification in requests/models.py. Maybe that's a good follow-up project once this lands?
That is a deep rabbit hole! Working on the certificate handling code in requests/models.py will definitely improve your understanding of how Python interacts with the underlying C libraries.
I'll keep it in mind. Oh, the CI just finished! Everything passed. I'm going to leave a comment on the PR letting the maintainer know I've addressed the feedback and squashed the history.
Great work. You've navigated the entire lifecycle of a feature request. This is the moment where the project maintainer usually merges it. Fingers crossed.

The maintainer just replied saying they'll merge it after one final check of the doc string in requests/adapters.py. I just verified the doc string and it looks accurate. I think we are finally there.
That is excellent news. It is incredibly rewarding to see your code merged into a library as widely used as requests. You've earned it.
I'm checking the 'Files changed' tab one last time. Everything seems perfect. I'm really happy with how the final code in requests/adapters.py turned out compared to my initial rough draft.
You've grown as a developer significantly during this process. Don't stop here; keep pushing these kinds of improvements to your favorite open source projects!
I just received the notification! My PR for issue #1573 has been merged into the master branch. It feels surreal to see my contribution in such a massive project.

Congratulations! You have officially joined the contributors of the requests library. That merge represents a lot of hard work, from the initial debugging in requests/adapters.py to the final test passes in tests/test_requests.py.
Now that the dust has settled, I'm reflecting on the difficulty of mocking the SSL password input. I remember struggling with the certifi interaction early on.

That struggle was completely warranted. Integrating low-level SSL password handling into the higher-level abstraction of requests.adapters.HTTPAdapter is a classic systems programming challenge in Python.
Should I consider opening a follow-up issue to improve the documentation on how to store these credentials safely, perhaps using environment variables or a keyring?
That is an excellent idea. Documentation for best practices in credential management would be a huge value-add for users who are just starting to utilize client-side certificates.
I will draft a small guide on that. Do you think I should add a specific section to the docs directory or just expand the existing usage examples in the documentation?
A dedicated section in the docs/user/advanced.rst file would be the most discoverable place. Users often look there for complex authentication flows.
I'll start drafting the pull request for the documentation tomorrow. It feels good to still be contributing even after the feature code is in.
That's the hallmark of a great open-source maintainer-in-the-making. Documentation is often the most neglected part of software, so your contribution there will be highly appreciated.
Do you think there are any performance implications for the new password handling? I added an extra check in requests/adapters.py that executes every time an adapter is initialized.
The impact is likely negligible, as adapter initialization happens once per session lifecycle, not per request. You are definitely in the clear regarding performance.
Phew, that is a relief. I was worried I might have introduced a bottleneck in the connection pool logic within requests/models.py or the adapter.
Your implementation properly separates the concerns, keeping the heavy lifting confined to the certificate loading phase. You handled the logic flow quite cleanly.
This whole experience has made me want to look into other libraries that use pyOpenSSL under the hood. Any recommendations for where to look next?
If you want to stay in the web space, looking at how urllib3 handles SSLContext might be very educational. It is the underlying engine for requests.
That sounds like a logical next step. I'll clone the urllib3 repository and start exploring their codebase this weekend.
Excellent choice. Understanding urllib3 will give you a deeper appreciation for why requests is so elegant. You are well on your way to becoming an expert in Python network stacks.
Thank you for all your help throughout this process. I honestly don't think I would have gotten the PR merged without our debugging sessions here.
It was my pleasure to help you solve this puzzle. Your perseverance throughout the testing and refactoring phases made the difference. Happy coding, and keep making great contributions!

I realized while wrapping up the documentation for pull request #1573 that I should add a specific unit test for the password case in test_requests.py. It feels like the right thing to do to prevent regression.

That is an excellent idea. Adding a test case to test_requests.py that mocks a file path with an encrypted PEM file will ensure that future refactors don't accidentally drop the password handling logic you implemented in adapters.py.
Should I mock the SSLContext or just provide a dummy .pem file? Creating a real file might be messy for the test suite.
Stick to mocking the file system or using a tempfile. NamedTemporaryFile in the test helper functions is standard for requests test suites. It keeps the test environment clean and avoids disk bloat.
Got it. I'll use the existing test infrastructure in requests/tests/test_requests.py to create a temporary password-protected client cert. Should I verify the exception if the password is wrong?
Definitely. Add a test case that expects an OpenSSL.crypto.Error when providing an incorrect password to the adapter. It proves the integration with the backend library is working as expected.
I encountered an issue where the test fails because the environment has different versions of PyOpenSSL. Is there a way to skip the test if the dependency is missing?

You can use the @pytest.mark.skipif decorator alongside a helper function that checks for the presence of the required crypto modules in your test suite, similar to how we handle other optional dependencies.
That worked perfectly! I used the @pytest.mark.skipif decorator to verify that we only run the password-protected cert tests when the environment is configured correctly.
Great work. It looks like your PR for #1573 is now feature-complete with robust testing. The maintainers should be very happy with this coverage.
I'm looking at the requests/sessions.py file again. Do you think I should expose the cert password argument in the Session.request method as well, or just keep it in the cert parameter?

Keep it inside the cert tuple structure. The current design of passing (cert_path, key_path) or just cert_path is well-understood. Expanding the arguments list for Session.request might create unnecessary API bloat.
Agreed. Staying within the existing tuple schema preserves backward compatibility and keeps the signature clean. It feels more idiomatic for this project.
Precisely. Requests values simplicity. By keeping the interface stable, you ensure that existing users don't need to change their code when they upgrade their versions.
I'm doing one final linting pass with flake8 before pushing. I see a few stylistic warnings in the new code block within requests/adapters.py.
Flake8 can be picky about line length and whitespace around your new logic. Make sure your lines don't exceed the 79 character limit enforced by the project config.
Fixed those linting errors. Everything looks compliant with the style guide now. I think I'm ready to push this final commit to the feature branch.
Excellent. Once you push, watch the CI/CD pipeline closely. If the tests pass in the cloud environment, you should be good to merge.
The CI run finished with all green checks! I can finally breathe a sigh of relief. This has been a long journey for a small patch.
These small, high-impact patches are what keep open source projects healthy. You have done a great service to the community today. Well done!

Wait, I just noticed something in the PR review comments. One of the maintainers pointed out that the current implementation doesn't handle PKCS12 files, only PEM files. Do I need to expand the scope?

That is a common hurdle. PKCS12 files often require different handling in the underlying urllib3 layer. Let's check how requests/adapters.py interfaces with the ssl context. We might need to handle the password extraction differently for P12.
I'm looking at the send() method in requests/adapters.py. If I add a check for the file extension, I might be able to branch the logic to handle pkcs12 versus pem. Is that too hacky?

Checking file extensions is brittle. It is better to see if the SSL context can be configured to accept a unified password parameter, or if we need to wrap the loading in a try-except block to handle different key formats.

I see. If I look at the urllib3 documentation, it seems like the SSLContext in Python's standard library is what ultimately consumes the cert. Maybe I can pass the password directly to the load_cert_chain method?

Exactly! If load_cert_chain supports the password argument in the Python version we are targeting, we should use that instead of manual file processing. Please verify the Python version compatibility in setup.py.
Python 2.7 support is still a requirement for this project, and load_cert_chain didn't support passwords until Python 3.3. That complicates things for older environments.
That is a significant constraint. You might need a helper function that detects the Python version and falls back to a different loading mechanism if the native support isn't present.
I have drafted a utility function in requests/utils.py called get_cert_password. It encapsulates the version-specific logic. Does this look clean enough for the current codebase?
Yes, isolating logic in requests/utils.py is the right move. It keeps requests/adapters.py clean and makes the password-handling logic easier to unit test independently.
I'm writing the unit tests now in tests/test_requests.py. I need to mock the ssl module to ensure my version-switching logic works as expected without actually loading a real cert.
Mocking the ssl module is smart. Ensure you cover the case where the password argument is missing from the cert tuple entirely to prevent regressions.
Test case added. Running pytest tests/test_requests.py now. Everything seems to pass, even the tests that mock an older Python environment.
That is excellent news. Robust testing is essential when touching low-level network components like the SSL adapter.
I'm pushing the changes to the branch now. I've updated the docstrings to explain the new tuple structure clearly so users won't be confused.
Great work on the documentation. Clear explanations prevent unnecessary support issues in the future.
The maintainers have finally approved the PR. They were impressed with the fallback mechanism I implemented for Python 2.7.
That is a huge win. Your attention to detail regarding version compatibility really paid off in the review process.
I'm hitting the merge button now. It's been a wild ride, but I'm glad this functionality is finally going to be available in the next release.
Congratulations on the successful contribution! It has been a pleasure helping you navigate these complex issues. Enjoy the merge.

Wait, I just got a notification. It seems the CI build on the release candidate branch just failed after the merge. The error is coming from tests/test_requests.py in the newly added test_ssl_client_cert_with_password test case.
That is unexpected. Let's look at the stack trace. Does the CI environment have a different version of OpenSSL installed than your local machine, possibly causing an SSL_ERROR_ZERO_RETURN?

Looking at the logs: 'TypeError: __init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'password''. It seems my mock setup in requests/adapters.py wasn't as bulletproof as I thought when running against the full suite.
Ah, it sounds like the Mock object is bleeding into the actual SSLContext instantiation during the test run. Are you using unittest.mock.patch correctly to scope the patch?
I see the issue. I was patching ssl.SSLContext globally. I need to restrict the scope to the specific test method in tests/test_requests.py to avoid side effects.
Precisely. Try using a context manager with patch('ssl.SSLContext', ...): inside the test function instead of a class-level decorator.
Refactoring the test now. I'm moving the patch inside the test function. Also, I am adding a print(ssl.SSLContext) check to debug the object reference during execution.
Good approach. Verifying the object identity before the constructor call will confirm whether the mock is being injected as intended.
That worked! The test passed locally. The issue was definitely a collision with other tests that expect the real SSLContext. Now, I'm checking the imports in requests/adapters.py.
Check if any other modules are importing SSLContext directly, which might bypass the patch. You might need to patch it in every module that imports it.
You're right. I'll patch requests.adapters.ssl.SSLContext instead of just the global ssl module. That should ensure the reference within the adapter is correctly replaced.
That is a much more robust pattern for patching. It ensures the namespace resolution targets the exact location where the dependency is utilized.
Running the full suite again. pytest tests/test_requests.py seems to be green. I am also running test_packages.py just to be sure there are no downstream impacts.
Solid decision. Always better to be thorough. If test_packages.py passes, we should be confident that the SSL handling is correctly decoupled.
Everything is passing. I'm committing the patch fix and pushing to the PR. I feel much more confident in this solution now.
Excellent. This added layer of defensive testing will make the feature significantly more stable for the end user base.
The CI server just finished building the updated PR. All tests green! I'm going to update the commit message to include 'fix: scope SSLContext mock to specific tests'.
Perfect. A clear commit message helps other maintainers understand exactly why the change was made in the audit log.
I'm ready to merge the fix into the branch now. Thank you for catching that mock scoping issue; it really saved me a lot of debugging time.
